# Apple Platform Design System: Animation, Motion, and Interaction

Self-contained. The skill's rules, then this topic, then anything it relies on from other skills.

## Skill rules

SwiftUI only. No UIKit unless explicitly required.

Baseline is iOS 27 / iPadOS 27 / macOS 27 Golden Gate, built with the Xcode 27 SDK. Code and design files both follow the 27 design language. There's no compatibility opt-out. Version numbers, dates, and what changed since 26 live only in [reference/platform-status.md](platform-status.md). Read it before quoting a version, before using an API marked (27) in a project that deploys to 26, and for any 26-era code or design file.

### Philosophy

Liquid Glass is a navigation-layer material. It floats above content. It does not touch content.

Three layers, in order:
1. Content (bottom): lists, media, text, cards. No glass.
2. Navigation (middle): toolbars, tab bars, sidebars, floating controls. Liquid Glass lives here.
3. Overlay (top): vibrancy, fills, and text rendered on glass surfaces.

If you're applying glass to content, you're doing it wrong. Cards are content. The API, the values, and the one system exception are in liquid-glass.md.

### Platform Visual Signature

A correct design is immediately recognizable as Apple-made. If it reads as a web app or as Android, it's wrong. Check this on nearly every task.

**What makes it immediately look like iOS:**
- Tab bar sits at the bottom of the screen with glass treatment, floating above content
- Content scrolls behind both the status bar at top and the tab bar at bottom (edge-to-edge)
- Navigation is push-based: screens slide left/right. Back button in the upper-left.
- Large title at the top of a navigation stack collapses as the user scrolls
- Partial-height sheets are inset from the screen edges, float with rounded corners and a glass background, and turn more opaque when expanded to full height
- SF Pro font throughout. No third-party fonts unless deliberately part of a brand decision.
- SF Symbols for all iconography. No custom icon libraries.
- Semantic colors. The background shifts automatically between light and dark.

**What makes it immediately look like macOS:**
- Standard window chrome (traffic light buttons top-left, window title centered or leading)
- Sidebar on the left with icon + label navigation, running edge-to-edge (top, bottom, and side of the window). Part of the window, not an inset floating panel. Icons take the accent color. In an inactive window, icons and text dim.
- Toolbar at the top with glass controls on the system's uniform toolbar treatment, the same in every app
- Window shape and corner radius are the system's. Contained elements are concentric with it. An app doesn't design its own window radius.
- Menus carry icons only where they clarify. Most menu items are text only.

**Wrong if:**
- Tab bar is at the top (that's web or Android)
- Navigation bar has a solid opaque background (content should extend behind it)
- Colors are hardcoded instead of semantic (system semantic colors, or the project's own semantic tokens)
- Icons are not SF Symbols
- Text fields, buttons, or lists look like generic HTML form controls
- There is no glass treatment on the navigation layer
- A partial-height sheet is flush to the screen edges with no inset rounding
- Safe areas are ignored (content or interactive elements under the status bar or in the home indicator zone)
- A Mac sidebar is drawn as an inset floating card, or a Mac toolbar's transparency is hand-tuned per screen (both are the 26 look)

## Topic

Apple-specific motion: what the platform already animates, glass, symbols, gestures, haptics, Reduce Motion.

Motion tokens aren't defined here. The `motion-design` skill owns them. Its `reference/cross-platform-tokens.md` defines `Motion.Spring.snappy`, `.standard`, `.expressive`, `.dragRelease` and `Motion.Ease.enter`, `.exit`, `.standard`, `.fade`, `.ambient`. Its `reference/ios-swiftui.md` has the SwiftUI animation API (springs, keyframes, phase animators, transitions). No raw spring or duration values at a call site.

### Contents

- [Core Principle](#core-principle)
- [Platform Rules](#platform-rules)
- [Liquid Glass Motion](#liquid-glass-motion)
- [Symbol Effects](#symbol-effects)
- [Gestures](#gestures)

### Core Principle

Motion communicates. It orients, confirms, and guides. It doesn't decorate.

Every animation answers one of these questions:
- Where did that go?
- What just happened?
- What can I do next?

If it doesn't answer any of those, cut it.

### Platform Rules

User-triggered motion gets a spring. System-triggered motion gets an ease token: enter for arrivals, exit for departures.

Match direction to spatial relationships: if a view slides in from the right, it dismisses to the right.

Never cut between states. The weight of the animation matches the weight of the change: `snappy` for small toggles, `standard` for layout changes, `expressive` for expanding and collapsing glass.

Elements materialize. They appear and disappear by modulating the material, not by popping in. Match that in custom transitions with opacity plus scale. No hard cuts.

Navigation pushes, sheets, the tab bar, toolbars, and menus already move correctly. Don't re-animate them.

### Liquid Glass Motion

Liquid Glass has its own physics. `.glassEffect(.regular.interactive())` adds scale on press, bounce, shimmer, and touch-point illumination, and on macOS a pointer response. Don't layer custom animations on top.

Morphing is user-triggered, so it gets a spring:

```swift
withAnimation(Motion.Spring.expressive) {
    isExpanded.toggle()
}
```

Set how a glass element enters and leaves with `glassEffectTransition(_:)` (`.matchedGeometry` or `.materialize`), not a hand-built transition. See `liquid-glass.md`.

### Symbol Effects

SF Symbols animate natively. Use the built-in effects before drawing anything custom.

```swift
// Swap one symbol for another (state toggle)
Image(systemName: isMuted ? "speaker.slash.fill" : "speaker.wave.2.fill")
    .contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))

// One-shot effect when a value changes
Image(systemName: "arrow.down.circle")
    .symbolEffect(.bounce, value: downloadCount)

// Ongoing effect while a condition holds
Image(systemName: "wifi")
    .symbolEffect(.variableColor.iterative, isActive: isConnecting)

// Number changes
Text(count, format: .number)
    .contentTransition(.numericText())
```

Available effects: `.bounce`, `.pulse`, `.scale`, `.variableColor`, `.appear`, `.disappear`, `.replace`, `.wiggle`, `.rotate`, `.breathe`, `.drawOn`, `.drawOff`.

Match the effect to the meaning: bounce confirms, pulse and breathe signal ongoing activity, variable color shows progress or strength, draw on suits completion. An indefinite effect stops when the state it describes ends.

### Gestures

Swipe to go back is a system behavior. Never remove or interfere with it.

Track the finger with no animation, then release into a spring so the drag's velocity carries over:

```swift
.gesture(
    DragGesture()
        .onChanged { value in offset = value.translation }
        .onEnded { _ in
            withAnimation(Motion.Spring.dragRelease) { offset = .zero }
        }
)
```

Selectable `Text` has its own selection gestures under the 27 SDK. If a custom gesture on it has to win, use `.highPriorityGesture()`.

### Haptics

Use system haptics for confirmations, errors, and selection changes. Never build a custom haptic when a system pattern exists. In SwiftUI that's `sensoryFeedback`, driven by the state change itself. No UIKit feedback generators.

```swift
// Selection
.sensoryFeedback(.selection, trigger: selectedTab)

// Impact
.sensoryFeedback(.impact(weight: .medium), trigger: dropCount)

// Outcome
.sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: saveCount)

// Only for some changes
.sensoryFeedback(trigger: phase) { _, new in
    new == .failed ? .error : nil
}
```

One haptic per event the user caused or needs to know about. Standard controls already play their own; don't double them.

### Reduce Motion

Always respect `accessibilityReduceMotion`. Replace spatial motion with opacity.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion

var transition: AnyTransition {
    reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .trailing).combined(with: .opacity)
}
```

System transitions and Liquid Glass adapt on their own. Custom motion doesn't: parallax, scroll effects, continuous loops, indefinite symbol effects, `TimelineView` drawing.

### From motion-design: Motion Tokens

This is the one definition of the motion token names and their values on every platform. The other files in this skill, and the `apple-platform`, `android-platform`, `web-platform`, and `visual-styles` skills, use these names and don't define their own. Change a value here and nowhere else.

Three families, matching the spring-vs-ease rule. **Spring tokens** for user-triggered motion. **Duration and easing tokens**, used together, for system-triggered motion. A project's design files or existing token set override the values. The names stay. A visual style can declare extra tokens in its own file under the same naming rule. A style-local token is a token, not an inline value.

##### Contents

- [Spring Tokens](#spring-tokens)
- [Duration Tokens](#duration-tokens)
- [Easing Tokens](#easing-tokens)
- [Definitions per Platform](#definitions-per-platform)
- [Reduced Motion Policy](#reduced-motion-policy)
- [Anti-Patterns](#anti-patterns)

##### Spring Tokens

One spring per token, written three ways. All three platforms run the same spring: mass 1, stiffness (2π / duration)², damping ratio 1 - bounce.

| Token | Use | Spring | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **snappy** | Press states, toggles, controls | 0.25s, bounce 0.15 | `Motion.Spring.snappy` | `Motion.Spring.snappy()` | `var(--spring-snappy)` over `var(--spring-snappy-duration)` |
| **standard** | Default for interactive elements: cards, sheets, menus, navigation | 0.35s, bounce 0 | `Motion.Spring.standard` | `Motion.Spring.standard()` | `var(--spring-standard)` over `var(--spring-standard-duration)` |
| **expressive** | Visible bounce: FABs, notifications, moments meant to delight | 0.4s, bounce 0.3 | `Motion.Spring.expressive` | `Motion.Spring.expressive()` | `var(--spring-expressive)` over `var(--spring-expressive-duration)` |
| **dragRelease** | An element let go after a drag, settling with the gesture's velocity | 0.3s, bounce 0.28 | `Motion.Spring.dragRelease` | `Motion.Spring.dragRelease()` | none: CSS can't inherit gesture velocity, so drag release on web is driven from JavaScript |

A spring's duration is perceptual, not its settle time. The CSS `--spring-*-duration` values (350ms, 520ms, 660ms) are settle times, which is why they're longer. Each CSS curve is only valid at its paired duration.

Android apps themed with Material 3 Expressive take component and component-like motion from `MaterialTheme.motionScheme` instead. See `android-platform`. `Motion.Spring.*()` is for custom motion the scheme doesn't cover.

##### Duration Tokens

For system-triggered motion, always paired with an easing token. Springs don't take a duration token.

| Token | Value | Use | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **micro** | 83ms | Feedback that isn't spring-driven: icon swaps, color flips | `Motion.Duration.micro` | `Motion.Duration.micro` | `var(--duration-micro)` |
| **fast** | 150ms | Small state changes, exits, fades | `Motion.Duration.fast` | `Motion.Duration.fast` | `var(--duration-fast)` |
| **standard** | 250ms | Most transitions: dropdown open, toast appear, content swap | `Motion.Duration.standard` | `Motion.Duration.standard` | `var(--duration-standard)` |
| **slow** | 350ms | Large layout shifts, full-screen transitions | `Motion.Duration.slow` | `Motion.Duration.slow` | `var(--duration-slow)` |
| **cinematic** | 600ms | Deliberate editorial moments, ambient loops | `Motion.Duration.cinematic` | `Motion.Duration.cinematic` | `var(--duration-cinematic)` |

Nothing shorter than **micro**. Below that, make the change instant. Nothing longer than **700ms** in product UI. If an animation needs longer to feel right, more motion isn't the fix. Scroll-scrubbed and ambient WebGL sequences have no duration of their own, so they're exempt.

##### Easing Tokens

| Token | Curve | Use | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **enter** | 0, 0, 0.2, 1 | Entrances: decelerates as it arrives | `Motion.Curve.enter` | `Motion.Ease.enter` | `var(--ease-enter)` |
| **exit** | 0.4, 0, 1, 1 | Exits: accelerates as it leaves | `Motion.Curve.exit` | `Motion.Ease.exit` | `var(--ease-exit)` |
| **standard** | 0.4, 0, 0.2, 1 | State changes that stay on screen | `Motion.Curve.standard` | `Motion.Ease.standard` | `var(--ease-standard)` |
| **emphasized** | 0.2, 0, 0, 1 | Quick start, long settle: hero and container moves | `Motion.Curve.emphasized` | `Motion.Ease.emphasized` | `var(--ease-emphasized)` |
| **expo-out** | 0.16, 1, 0.3, 1 | Very fast start, very long tail: reveals | `Motion.Curve.expoOut` | `Motion.Ease.expoOut` | `var(--ease-expo-out)` |
| **sine-in-out** | 0.45, 0.05, 0.55, 0.95 | Gentle and symmetrical: slow, ambient | `Motion.Curve.sineInOut` | `Motion.Ease.sineInOut` | `var(--ease-sine-in-out)` |

Linear isn't a token. It's only right for continuous loops and scroll-linked motion.

Swift is the one exception to the naming rule. SwiftUI animations carry their duration, so `motion/ease/<name>` becomes two things: `Motion.Curve.<name>` is the bare curve, and `Motion.Ease.<name>` is the ready-to-use `Animation`, the curve at its default duration. The pairs are `Motion.Ease.enter` (enter, standard), `exit` (exit, fast), `standard` (standard, standard), `emphasized` (emphasized, slow), `expoOut` (expo-out, cinematic), `fade` (enter, fast), and `ambient` (sine-in-out, cinematic). In Kotlin `Motion.Ease.enter`, `exit`, and `standard` alias Compose's `LinearOutSlowInEasing`, `FastOutLinearInEasing`, and `FastOutSlowInEasing`. Call sites use the token name.

##### Definitions per Platform

One definition site per platform. Call sites reference the token, never a raw curve, duration, or spring constant.

```css
:root {
    --duration-micro: 83ms;
    --duration-fast: 150ms;
    --duration-standard: 250ms;
    --duration-slow: 350ms;
    --duration-cinematic: 600ms;

    --ease-enter: cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1);
    --ease-exit: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);
    --ease-standard: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
    --ease-emphasized: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);
    --ease-expo-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
    --ease-sine-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.45, 0.05, 0.55, 0.95);

    /* Springs as linear() stops: mass 1, stiffness (2π / duration)²,
       damping ratio 1 - bounce, sampled to the point the spring settles
       within 0.1%. */

    /* snappy: duration 0.25s, bounce 0.15 (stiffness 632, damping ratio 0.85) */
    --spring-snappy: linear(0, 0.006 1.2%, 0.026 2.8%, 0.057 4.2%, 0.096 5.8%, 0.191 8.8%, 0.413 15%, 0.514 18%, 0.613 21.2%, 0.698 24.5%, 0.765 27.5%, 0.825 30.8%, 0.873 34%, 0.914 37.5%, 0.946 41.2%, 0.971 45.5%, 0.989 50.2%, 1 55.8%, 1.006 67.8%, 1);
    --spring-snappy-duration: 350ms;

    /* standard: duration 0.35s, bounce 0 (stiffness 322, damping ratio 1) */
    --spring-standard: linear(0, 0.004 1%, 0.019 2.2%, 0.043 3.5%, 0.08 5%, 0.156 7.5%, 0.367 13.8%, 0.463 16.8%, 0.557 20%, 0.638 23.2%, 0.707 26.5%, 0.769 30%, 0.819 33.5%, 0.862 37.2%, 0.901 41.8%, 0.93 46.5%, 0.954 52%, 0.972 58.2%, 0.984 65.2%, 0.992 73.5%, 1);
    --spring-standard-duration: 520ms;

    /* expressive: duration 0.4s, bounce 0.3 (stiffness 247, damping ratio 0.7), 4.6% overshoot */
    --spring-expressive: linear(0, 0.008 1.2%, 0.03 2.5%, 0.063 3.8%, 0.114 5.2%, 0.218 7.8%, 0.476 13.2%, 0.587 15.8%, 0.697 18.5%, 0.783 21%, 0.855 23.5%, 0.918 26.2%, 0.966 29%, 1.003 32%, 1.022 34.2%, 1.036 36.8%, 1.044 39.5%, 1.046 42.5%, 1.041 47.8%, 1.012 62.3%, 1.003 70%, 0.998 81.8%, 1);
    --spring-expressive-duration: 660ms;

    --motion-distance-sm: 12px;
    --motion-distance-md: 24px;
}
```

```swift
import SwiftUI

enum Motion {
    enum Duration {
        static let micro: TimeInterval = 0.083
        static let fast: TimeInterval = 0.15
        static let standard: TimeInterval = 0.25
        static let slow: TimeInterval = 0.35
        static let cinematic: TimeInterval = 0.6
    }

    enum Curve {
        static let enter = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 1))
        static let exit = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.4, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 1, y: 1))
        static let standard = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.4, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 1))
        static let emphasized = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0, y: 1))
        static let expoOut = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.16, y: 1), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.3, y: 1))
        static let sineInOut = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.45, y: 0.05), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.55, y: 0.95))
    }

    enum Spring {
        static let snappy = Animation.snappy(duration: 0.25)                 // bounce 0.15
        static let standard = Animation.spring(duration: 0.35, bounce: 0)
        static let expressive = Animation.spring(duration: 0.4, bounce: 0.3)
        static let dragRelease = Animation.spring(duration: 0.3, bounce: 0.28)
    }

    enum Ease {
        static let enter = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.enter, duration: Duration.standard)
        static let exit = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.exit, duration: Duration.fast)
        static let standard = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.standard, duration: Duration.standard)
        static let emphasized = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.emphasized, duration: Duration.slow)
        static let expoOut = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.expoOut, duration: Duration.cinematic)
        static let fade = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.enter, duration: Duration.fast)
        static let ambient = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.sineInOut, duration: Duration.cinematic)
    }
}
```

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.animation.core.CubicBezierEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.Easing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.FastOutLinearInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.FastOutSlowInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.LinearOutSlowInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.SpringSpec
import androidx.compose.animation.core.spring

object Motion {
    object Spring {
        fun <T> snappy(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.85f, stiffness = 632f)
        fun <T> standard(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 1f, stiffness = 322f)
        fun <T> expressive(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.7f, stiffness = 247f)
        fun <T> dragRelease(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.72f, stiffness = 439f)
    }

    object Duration {
        const val micro = 83
        const val fast = 150
        const val standard = 250
        const val slow = 350
        const val cinematic = 600
    }

    object Ease {
        val enter: Easing = LinearOutSlowInEasing
        val exit: Easing = FastOutLinearInEasing
        val standard: Easing = FastOutSlowInEasing
        val emphasized: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.2f, 0f, 0f, 1f)
        val expoOut: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.16f, 1f, 0.3f, 1f)
        val sineInOut: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.45f, 0.05f, 0.55f, 0.95f)
    }
}
```

Usage:

```css
.button { transition: scale var(--spring-snappy-duration) var(--spring-snappy); }
.toast  { transition: opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter); }
```
```swift
withAnimation(Motion.Spring.standard) { isExpanded.toggle() }
```
```kotlin
animateFloatAsState(target, animationSpec = Motion.Spring.snappy(), label = "scale")
tween<Float>(durationMillis = Motion.Duration.standard, easing = Motion.Ease.enter)
```

GSAP registers the easing tokens under the same names (`"enter"`, `"expo-out"`, and so on). See [gsap.md](../motion-design/gsap.md#setup).

##### Reduced Motion Policy

The policy lives here. Each platform file only shows the API that reads the setting. The reasons are in [foundations.md](../motion-design/foundations.md#why-reduced-motion-matters).

When the user asks for reduced motion:

- **Spatial motion becomes a fade.** Replace slides, zooms, scale, and shared-element travel with an opacity change at **fast** with **enter** (`Motion.Ease.fade`), or an instant change.
- **Springs lose their bounce.** Where a spring stays (a control following a finger), use **standard**, never **expressive**.
- **Scroll-linked motion goes.** No parallax, no scroll-driven transforms, no pinned or scrubbed sequences. Content sits in its final position. Smooth scrolling is off.
- **Autoplaying and looping decoration stops.** A spinner that says "working" can stay.
- **Feedback stays.** Color, opacity, and state changes still happen. Reduced motion never means a control gives no response.

Android's "Remove animations" goes further. It zeroes the animator duration scale, so Compose animations jump to their end state and no substitute fade runs. See [android-compose.md](../motion-design/android-compose.md#reduce-motion).

##### Anti-Patterns

**Linear motion on interactive elements.** Nothing physical moves at constant velocity. Use a spring or an ease.

**Identical timing for all properties.** Opacity that finishes slightly before position reads as one arrival. Opacity that finishes long before it shows the destination before the journey is over.

**Animating layout properties.** `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding` trigger layout every frame. Animate render-time properties: `transform`/`translate`/`scale` and `opacity` on web, `scaleEffect`/`offset` in SwiftUI, `graphicsLayer` in Compose.

**Interrupting without velocity handoff.** When a user reverses direction mid-flight, the new animation has to pick up the current velocity. Springs do. Duration-based animations restart from rest.

**Staggering too much.** 30-60ms between items creates rhythm. 150ms makes the UI feel slow. Stagger the first several items and bring the rest in together.

**Decorative animation on high-frequency paths.** Press feedback is **snappy** or **micro**, nothing longer.

**Parallax on critical content.** It can't be what positions content a user needs to read.

**Inline motion values.** A raw `cubic-bezier()`, a bare millisecond count, or spring constants at a call site.

**Not testing interruption.** Tap, release, tap again rapidly. Swipe, reverse, swipe again. If it breaks, it's duration-based where it should be a spring, or it restarts from a hard-coded start value.

**Skipping reduced motion.** Test every animated surface with the system setting on.

### From motion-design: iOS / SwiftUI Motion

SwiftUI animation for iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. `Motion.*` is the token enum from [cross-platform-tokens.md](../motion-design/cross-platform-tokens.md#definitions-per-platform). Use it. No literal springs or durations in views. HIG motion rules, Liquid Glass morphing, and haptics are in the `apple-platform` skill.

##### Status

The OS baseline, SDK status, and what changed between releases live in `apple-platform/reference/platform-status.md`. The `.zoom` and `.crossFade` navigation transitions are iOS and iPadOS only. They're unavailable on macOS.

##### Spring API

These are the forms you'll meet when reading or defining tokens. The presets are fixed bounces on `.spring(duration:bounce:)`, all with a default duration of 0.5:

```swift
.smooth                               // bounce 0
.snappy                               // bounce 0.15
.bouncy                               // bounce 0.3
.snappy(duration: 0.2)                // each preset takes duration and extraBounce
.bouncy(duration: 0.4, extraBounce: 0.2)

.spring(duration: 0.3, bounce: 0.2)   // bounce 0 = critically damped, > 0 overshoots,
                                      // < 0 = overdamped, flatter

// Older form, still common in existing code.
// duration == response, bounce == 1 - dampingFraction.
.spring(response: 0.35, dampingFraction: 0.7)
```

`duration` is perceptual, not the settle time. To run code when the motion has actually finished, use the completion form:

```swift
withAnimation(Motion.Spring.standard) {
    isExpanded = true
} completion: {
    focusField()
}
```

##### Which Token Where

| Situation | Token |
| --- | --- |
| Press feedback, toggles, small controls | `Motion.Spring.snappy` |
| Sheets, cards, menus, navigation, list insert and delete | `Motion.Spring.standard` |
| Releasing a dragged element | `Motion.Spring.dragRelease` |
| Badge pop, playful emphasis | `Motion.Spring.expressive` |
| Loading and ambient loops | `Motion.Ease.ambient` |
| System-triggered appear and disappear | `Motion.Ease.enter`, `Motion.Ease.exit` |

##### Implicit vs Explicit Animations

```swift
// Implicit: attached to a view, runs when the watched value changes.
// For a single view reacting to its own state.
RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: Radius.lg)
    .scaleEffect(isActive ? 1.05 : 1.0)
    .animation(Motion.Spring.snappy, value: isActive)

// Explicit: wraps the state change; everything depending on that state
// animates together. For event-driven, multi-view changes.
Button("Expand") {
    withAnimation(Motion.Spring.standard) {
        isExpanded.toggle()
    }
}
```

Always pass `value:` to `.animation`. The form without it animates every change to the view, including ones you didn't intend, and is deprecated.

##### Gestures and Velocity

Springs carry velocity across interruption. Retarget a property that's mid-spring and it continues from its current speed. Gesture callbacks also track velocity automatically, so a spring started in `onEnded` begins at the speed the finger was moving.

```swift
@State private var offset: CGSize = .zero

card
    .offset(offset)
    .gesture(
        DragGesture()
            .onChanged { value in
                offset = value.translation          // no animation while tracking the finger
            }
            .onEnded { _ in
                withAnimation(Motion.Spring.dragRelease) {
                    offset = .zero                  // starts with the drag's velocity
                }
            }
    )
```

`DragGesture.Value.velocity` is there when the release behavior itself depends on speed, like dismissing on a fast flick.

##### Keyframe Animations

For multi-step choreography a single spring can't describe. Each track animates one property on its own timeline. The segment durations are the choreography and stay literal.

```swift
struct PopValues {
    var scale = 1.0
    var offsetY = 0.0
}

CardView()
    .keyframeAnimator(initialValue: PopValues(), trigger: isActive) { content, value in
        content
            .scaleEffect(value.scale)
            .offset(y: value.offsetY)
    } keyframes: { _ in
        KeyframeTrack(\.scale) {
            CubicKeyframe(0.95, duration: 0.1)     // quick compress
            SpringKeyframe(1.02, duration: 0.2)    // spring past rest
            SpringKeyframe(1.0, duration: 0.15)    // settle
        }
        KeyframeTrack(\.offsetY) {
            CubicKeyframe(-8, duration: 0.15)
            SpringKeyframe(0, duration: 0.3)
        }
    }
```

`LinearKeyframe` interpolates straight, `CubicKeyframe` curves through its neighbors, `SpringKeyframe` springs toward the value, `MoveKeyframe` jumps.

Keyframe animations play to completion and don't hand off velocity when interrupted. They're for one-shot choreography, never for something the user can grab mid-flight. The content closure runs every frame. Keep it cheap.

##### PhaseAnimator

Steps through discrete states, continuously or once per trigger. This is system-driven motion, so it takes an ease token.

```swift
// Continuous: loading indicator
LoadingDot()
    .phaseAnimator([false, true]) { content, isActive in
        content
            .scaleEffect(isActive ? 1.3 : 1.0)
            .opacity(isActive ? 0.6 : 1.0)
    } animation: { _ in
        Motion.Ease.ambient
    }

// Once per trigger: confirmation pulse
Image(systemName: "checkmark.circle.fill")
    .phaseAnimator([1.0, 1.2, 1.0], trigger: saveCount) { content, scale in
        content.scaleEffect(scale)
    }
```

##### Shared Element and Navigation Transitions

`matchedGeometryEffect` morphs between two views in the same hierarchy that share an ID. Only one of them can be in the hierarchy at a time. Rendering both breaks the animation.

```swift
@Namespace private var heroNamespace

if !isExpanded {
    Thumbnail(item)
        .matchedGeometryEffect(id: item.id, in: heroNamespace)
        .onTapGesture {
            withAnimation(Motion.Spring.standard) { isExpanded = true }
        }
} else {
    Detail(item)
        .matchedGeometryEffect(id: item.id, in: heroNamespace)
}
```

Across a navigation push or a presentation, use the zoom navigation transition instead (iOS and iPadOS). It's interactive, interruptible, and follows the dismiss gesture:

```swift
@Namespace private var namespace

NavigationLink {
    DetailView(item)
        .navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID: item.id, in: namespace))
} label: {
    Thumbnail(item)
        .matchedTransitionSource(id: item.id, in: namespace)
}
```

For a sheet that should appear in place instead of sliding up, use the cross-fade transition (iOS and iPadOS). `AnyNavigationTransition` type-erases a transition chosen at runtime.

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showDetail) {
    DetailSheet()
        .presentationDetents([.medium])
        .navigationTransition(.crossFade)
}
```

##### Symbol Effects and Content Transitions

SF Symbols animate through `symbolEffect`. Don't hand-build scale and rotation for what a symbol effect already does.

```swift
// Discrete: plays once each time the value changes
Image(systemName: "bell.fill")
    .symbolEffect(.bounce, value: notificationCount)

// Indefinite: runs while active
Image(systemName: "arrow.triangle.2.circlepath")
    .symbolEffect(.rotate, isActive: isSyncing)

// Swapping one symbol for another
Image(systemName: isMuted ? "speaker.slash.fill" : "speaker.wave.2.fill")
    .contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))

// Text that changes value: animate the digits, not a cross-fade of the label
Text(total, format: .number)
    .contentTransition(.numericText())
    .animation(Motion.Spring.snappy, value: total)
```

Effects: `appear`, `disappear`, `bounce`, `pulse`, `scale`, `variableColor`, `replace`, `wiggle`, `rotate`, `breathe`, `drawOn`, `drawOff`.

##### Reordering

Drag-to-reorder works in any stack, grid, list, or custom layout. The system supplies the lift, the moving placeholder, and the drop animation. Don't build this by hand.

```swift
VStack {
    ForEach(landmarks) { landmark in
        LandmarkRow(landmark)
    }
    .reorderable()
}
.reorderContainer(for: Landmark.self) { difference in
    let moved = landmarks.filter { difference.sources.contains($0.id) }
    landmarks.removeAll { difference.sources.contains($0.id) }
    switch difference.destination.position {
    case .before(let id):
        let index = landmarks.firstIndex { $0.id == id } ?? landmarks.endIndex
        landmarks.insert(contentsOf: moved, at: index)
    case .end:
        landmarks.append(contentsOf: moved)
    }
}
```

Containers holding several collections use `reorderable(collectionID:)` and `reorderContainer(for:in:isEnabled:move:)`.

##### @Animatable Macro

Synthesizes `animatableData` from a type's stored properties, replacing hand-written `AnimatablePair` nesting:

```swift
@Animatable
struct WaveShape: Shape {
    var amplitude: Double
    var frequency: Double
    var phase: Double
    @AnimatableIgnored var isMirrored: Bool   // excluded from interpolation

    func path(in rect: CGRect) -> Path {
        Path()   // draw using amplitude, frequency, phase
    }
}
```

##### Performance

Built-in animatable modifiers (`.scaleEffect()`, `.opacity()`, `.rotationEffect()`, `.offset()`) are cheap. SwiftUI interpolates them without re-running your view code. A custom `Animatable` type, a keyframe content closure, or a `TimelineView` re-evaluates on the main thread every frame, at up to 120Hz. Keep layout-heavy subtrees, data access, and formatting out of anything that re-evaluates per frame.

When a parent's size animates and its children jump instead of following, add `.geometryGroup()` to the parent.

##### Reduce Motion

The policy is in [cross-platform-tokens.md](../motion-design/cross-platform-tokens.md#reduced-motion-policy).

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion

// Replace spatial motion with a crossfade
var transition: AnyTransition {
    reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .trailing).combined(with: .opacity)
}

// Swap an expressive spring for the fade token
withAnimation(reduceMotion ? Motion.Ease.fade : Motion.Spring.expressive) {
    isPresented = true
}
```

System navigation and sheet transitions adapt on their own. Custom motion doesn't. Parallax, `scrollTransition` effects, continuous `PhaseAnimator` loops, indefinite symbol effects, and keyframes all need the check.
